explanation: ANCIENT means very old, so its opposite is modern. Historic also describes the past, so it points the same way rather than opposite.
A generous person gives freely; a miserly person hates to give or spend. Wealth is not the opposite, since rich people may be either.
EXPAND means to grow larger, so shrink is its opposite. Widen is a near-synonym.
Victory is winning; defeat is losing. Glory usually accompanies victory, and battle and struggle are the contest itself.
To arrive is to reach a place; to depart is to leave it. Waiting and pausing happen after arriving, and entering is close in meaning.
An honest person tells the truth; a deceitful person lies and cheats. Careful, friendly and modest describe other traits and do not oppose honesty.
DIFFICULT means hard to do, so easy is the opposite. Tough is a synonym.
Something empty holds nothing; something full holds as much as it can. Open, broken and clean describe other conditions.
To increase is to make greater; to decrease is to make less. The other verbs do not reverse the idea.
To accept an offer is to take it; to refuse is to turn it down. Admit can mean to accept as true, so it leans the same way.
Shallow water has little depth; deep water has a lot. Narrow concerns width, not depth.
Temporary things last a short time; permanent things last. Brief is a synonym of temporary.
FRAGILE means easily broken, so sturdy (strong, solid) is its opposite. Delicate is a synonym.
RAPID means fast, so slow is the opposite. Swift is a synonym, and sudden means unexpected, not slow.
A loyal friend stays faithful; an unfaithful one betrays. Obedient is related to following orders but is not the reverse of loyalty.
Scarce things are in short supply; plentiful things are available in large amounts. Precious and costly are often caused by scarcity, not opposed to it.
To ascend is to go up; to descend is to come down. Climb is a synonym.
A cheerful mood is happy and bright; a gloomy one is sad and dark. Calm, cautious and lazy are unrelated to mood in this sense.
A complex problem has many parts; a simple one has few. Tangled is close to complex in meaning.
To praise is to speak well of someone; to criticise is to point out faults. Thank and admire are positive like praise.
The majority is the larger part of a whole; the minority is the smaller part. Crowd and group do not state a size relation.
Visible means able to be seen; hidden means kept out of sight. Clear can describe a visible object, so it does not oppose it.
A genuine banknote is real; a fake one is a copy. Rare and precious may describe genuine things but say nothing about being real.
An innocent person has done no wrong; a guilty person has. Foolish, young and weak are not legal or moral opposites of innocence.
A humble person does not think too highly of himself; an arrogant person does. Poor describes money, and quiet describes manner of speaking.
To encourage is to give courage or hope; to discourage is to take it away. Support is a synonym.
To advance is to move forward; to retreat is to move back. Attack may involve advancing, so it is not opposite.
To destroy is to ruin completely; to build is to make. Attack, sink and scatter describe kinds of damage, not the reverse.
Something frequent happens often; something rare happens seldom. Regular is a near-synonym.
A wealthy person has much money; a poor person has little. Generous, mighty and famous are about character or status, not money.
BENEVOLENT means wishing good to others; malevolent means wishing harm. Charitable is a synonym of benevolent.
A candid reply is frank and open; an evasive one avoids the point. Blunt is close in meaning to candid because it also speaks plainly.
A diligent worker takes steady care over his duties; a negligent one fails to. Thorough is similar to diligent.
An optimist expects good outcomes; a pessimist expects bad ones. A realistic person expects whatever is likely, which is neither extreme.
Light passes through a transparent material; an opaque one blocks it. Clear is a synonym.
A voluntary act is done by choice; a compulsory one is required. Casual, generous and temporary do not concern choice.
An amateur works at something for pleasure rather than as a paid career; a professional does it for a living. A beginner may be a professional newly started, so it is not the contrary.
To conceal is to hide; to reveal is to show. Cover and disguise are ways of hiding, so they are synonyms.
To elevate is to raise; to lower is to bring down. Lift is a synonym.
A hostile person behaves like an enemy; a friendly one behaves like a friend. Distant describes coldness but not active enmity.
Inferior means lower in quality or rank; superior means higher. Minor and shabby are close to inferior.
A novice is new to a skill; an expert has long experience. A pupil is also learning, so pupil is closer to novice.
To prosper is to succeed and grow wealthy; to decline is to weaken or fall away. Trade and persist may accompany prosperity but do not reverse it.
A reluctant helper is unwilling; a willing one is glad to help. Doubtful is close to reluctant.
STAGNANT describes something still and unchanging; dynamic describes something full of movement and change. Calm is a related idea, and murky and shallow describe water quality.
SUPERFLUOUS means more than is needed; essential means absolutely needed. Excessive is close to superfluous.
A trivial matter is of little importance; a significant one matters a great deal. Brief and simple describe length and difficulty, not importance.
A virtue is a good moral quality; a vice is a bad one. Reward, honour and duty are not moral qualities of the same kind.
Weary means tired; energetic means full of energy. Anxious, patient and lonely are feelings that are unrelated to tiredness.
Zeal is passionate eagerness; apathy is a complete lack of interest. Anger and courage are strong feelings, but they are not the lack of eagerness.
Brittle material snaps instead of bending; flexible material bends without breaking. A solid object may still be brittle.
COARSE describes a rough texture, such as coarse flour; fine describes a smooth one. Rough is a synonym.
To deflate a tyre is to let air out; to inflate is to fill it with air. Flatten and empty point to the same result as deflate.
Fertile land supports crops; barren land cannot. Rich is a synonym in this context.
Gloomy weather is dark and depressing; sunny weather is bright. Dim is close in meaning to gloomy.
A hasty decision is made too quickly; a deliberate one is made after thought. Careless often accompanies hasty actions.
A jovial person is cheerful and friendly; a morose person is gloomy and silent. Witty and lively are also lively traits and do not oppose jovial.
A lavish meal is abundant and expensive; a meagre one is small and poor. Rich and wasteful lean toward lavish.
MUNDANE means ordinary and everyday; extraordinary means far beyond the ordinary. Tedious often describes mundane tasks.
A neutral referee takes no side; a biased one favours a side. Fair is a synonym.
An obedient child follows rules; a rebellious one resists them. Loyal and quiet are not opposites of following orders.
PROFOUND means deep in thought or feeling; superficial means concerned only with the surface. Intense and serious fit with profound.
To repel is to drive away; to attract is to draw closer. Chase also drives something away.
A solitary person prefers to be alone; a sociable one enjoys company. Lonely means being alone as well.
A timid person lacks confidence to act; a bold one acts with confidence. Nervous is a synonym.
A vague answer lacks clear detail; a precise one gives exact detail. Fuzzy is close in meaning.
Adversity is hardship and bad luck; prosperity is success and good fortune. Misfortune is a synonym.
To assemble is to bring together; to scatter is to spread apart. Gather means almost the same as assemble.
To condemn is to express strong disapproval; to praise is to express approval. Blame is a synonym.
Enmity is deep hostility between people; friendship is the warm bond between them. Rivalry and hatred are close to enmity.
FEEBLE means lacking strength; robust means strong and healthy. Sickly is a synonym.
A gradual change happens little by little; a sudden change happens all at once. Steady is a near-synonym.
Harmony is agreement or pleasing combination; discord is disagreement or clashing. Agreement is a synonym.
To kindle a fire is to set it burning; to extinguish is to put it out. Fuel is what keeps it burning, so it supports kindling.
A lucrative business earns a great deal; an unprofitable one earns little or loses money. Popular, risky and stable do not describe profit.
To permit is to allow; to forbid is to prohibit. Admit can mean allow in, so it fits with permit.
A rigid rule cannot be bent; a flexible one can. Strict is a synonym of rigid in this sense.
A sincere person means what he says; a hypocritical person pretends. Polite, gentle and formal describe manners, not honesty.
A tedious task is boring; an exciting one holds interest. Lengthy often goes with tedious.
To abolish a custom is to put an end to it; to establish is to set it up. Cancel is a synonym.
A garrulous person talks too much; a taciturn person says very little. Friendly, boastful and witty describe speech content, not amount.
A magnanimous person is generous in forgiving; a petty person is mean and holds small grudges. Lavish means spending much, which is not the same thing.
An obstinate person refuses to change his mind; a compliant person yields. Stubborn is a synonym.
A recalcitrant pupil resists authority; a docile one is easy to manage. Defiant is a synonym.
SPURIOUS means false while pretending to be real; authentic means genuine. Doubtful describes a reaction to something spurious.
A taciturn man says little; a talkative one says much. Gloomy and rude describe mood and manners, and shy describes nervousness, not the amount of talk.
UBIQUITOUS means found everywhere; rare means found in few places. Obscure means little known, not scarce in number.
A verbose writer uses too many words; a concise writer uses just enough. Formal, clear and fluent do not describe length.
A benign tumour is harmless; a malignant one is dangerous. Gentle is a synonym of benign in its general sense.
A capricious person changes his mind without reason; a constant person remains steady. Cunning, fierce and nimble do not describe steadiness.
A dearth of food is a serious shortage; an abundance is a large supply. Decline, greed and quarrel do not describe quantity.
INDIGENT means extremely poor; affluent means rich. Idle, foreign and thrifty describe other things than wealth.
To mitigate is to make less severe; to aggravate is to make worse. Settle may suggest solving rather than reversing.
Ostentatious behaviour is designed to attract attention and admiration; an unassuming person avoids display. Splendid describes grand display, so it leans the same way.
To venerate is to hold in deep respect; to despise is to regard with contempt. Admire is a synonym of weaker degree.
To wane is to become smaller or weaker, as the moon does after full moon; to grow is to become larger. Fade is a synonym.
The zenith is the highest point; the nadir is the lowest. Apex is a synonym.
SPARSE means thinly spread, such as sparse vegetation; dense means crowded closely together. Scattered is close in meaning to sparse.
A hospitable host receives guests warmly; an unwelcoming one makes them feel unwanted. Polite, wealthy and quiet describe other qualities.
The interior is the inside of something; the exterior is the outside. Central and hidden lean toward inside.
BRAVE means ready to face danger, so cowardly is its opposite. Fierce is a different quality (wild or aggressive), not a lack of courage.
A cruel person causes pain without pity; a kind person shows care. A strict person is firm but not necessarily cruel, and bitter is similar to cruel.
To commence is to begin; to conclude is to end. Continue means to carry on after beginning, which is not the reverse.
A smooth surface has no bumps; a rough surface has many. A flat surface can still be rough.
To widen is to make broader; to narrow is to make less broad. Lengthen and deepen add to a different dimension, and brighten concerns light.
FRUGAL means careful with money; extravagant means spending too freely. Thrifty is a synonym, and stingy leans the same way.
To abstain is to hold oneself back from something; to indulge is to give oneself fully to it. Refuse resembles abstain, so it is not opposite.
IMMENSE means extremely large; tiny means extremely small. Solid, ancient and dense do not describe size.
To unite is to bring together; to divide is to split apart. Join and rally are synonyms.
Jubilant means joyful with triumph; dejected means low in spirits. Angry is negative but not the reverse of joy in the same way.
ALACRITY is cheerful readiness to act; reluctance is unwillingness. Speed is related to alacrity, so it is not opposite.
EPHEMERAL means lasting only a very short time; enduring means lasting for a long time. Fleeting is a synonym.
PARSIMONIOUS means extremely unwilling to spend; prodigal means spending wastefully. Prudent describes careful judgement, not spending style.
An equivocal answer can be taken in more than one way; an unambiguous one has a single clear meaning. Doubtful is close to equivocal.
A prudent driver thinks of risk; a reckless driver ignores it. Stingy refers to spending, not judgement.
